# Luke 13: Research notes for the verse-by-verse commentary

**How to read these notes:** Each point gives its source page. I had a limited number of searches and page reads, so there are gaps. I found nothing on bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org, newadvent.org, oca.org or catholic.com, and nothing on prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace readings of this chapter. Those sections are left out rather than guessed. The only Catholic source I found is Haydock (v. 24). I couldn't open the Gill, Coffman or Ligonier pages; their points come only from short search-result extracts and should be checked before they go to print.

---

## 1. The traditional reading, verse by verse

**v. 1:** Guzik says no secular history records this exact event. He cites Barclay on a similar massacre (Pilate's agents with daggers among Jews protesting the use of temple money for an aqueduct) to show the act fits Pilate's character. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- The Pulpit Commentary thinks the people reporting it may have been watchers from Jerusalem. It cites Josephus on several Passover massacres under Roman rule. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- Wesley thinks the victims were followers of Judas Gaulonites who refused Roman authority, and Pilate killed them while they worshipped in the temple at a feast. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm

**vv. 2–3:** Guzik: Jesus doesn't say the victims were innocent, only that they were no *more* guilty than anyone else, because all are guilty. He turns the question from "why did this happen?" to "what does it mean for me?" https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- The Pulpit Commentary: the Lord rejects the unloving habit of treating one person's misfortune as punishment for that person's sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**vv. 3 and 5, what "perish" means (commentators disagree):**
- **The same kind of death, fulfilled in AD 70.** Wesley says the Greek means they would perish in the very same manner, and they did. The nation's best men were cut down by Roman swords at a festival, and many died in the temple. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/luke-13.html
  - Coffman also says the words mean Israel would die by the Roman sword, as the Galileans had. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-13.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary calls the words prophetic "to the letter": Jerusalem fell within forty years. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- **Eternal judgment.** Precept Austin says Jesus is not saying the hearers would die in the same horrible way or as suddenly. His point is that they will not escape God's judgment, which means perishing forever. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-13-commentary
- **Both.** The Light of Israel commentary sees both a threat of personal spiritual ruin and the physical destruction of the city. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/13-3.html

**vv. 3 and 5, "repent" twice:** Guzik argues from the Greek verb tenses that there are two kinds of repentance, both needed: once-for-all repentance (v. 5) and continuing repentance (v. 3). https://enduringword.com/feed/

**v. 4:** The Pulpit Commentary cites Ewald's guess that strict Jews saw the tower's fall as punishment, because Pilate paid the workers from sacred temple money. The work was probably on the aqueduct to the Pool of Siloam. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**vv. 6–7:** Guzik: God looks for fruit, beginning with the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the fig tree as Israel. On the "three years" it lists several views:
  - three periods of Israel's history;
  - Jesus' three years of ministry;
  - God's calls through the Law, the Prophets and Christ.
  
  It concludes that three most likely stands for full and complete opportunity, and that small details shouldn't be pushed too far. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- Wesley gives two options: the owner is God the Father and the gardener is Christ, or Christ owns the vineyard and his ministers tend it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm

**vv. 8–9:** Guzik: the story shows God's patience, but also his justice, because a day of reckoning finally comes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- The Pulpit Commentary takes the extra year as Israel's last time of grace: John the Baptist, Jesus' ministry and forty years of apostolic preaching. It quotes Professor Bruce: God's patience can run out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**v. 10:** The Pulpit Commentary mentions the suggestion that Jesus may by now have been shut out of some synagogues by a minor form of excommunication. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**v. 11:**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the exact description reflects Luke's medical training. It calls the illness a severe curvature of the spine, and takes her presence in synagogue as a sign of her faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- Guzik: spiritual causes don't explain *all* illness, but they can explain some. He cites Pate, who identifies the condition as a fusion of the spinal bones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

**vv. 12–13:** Guzik: Jesus speaks with both compassion and authority. The touch was a deliberate act of sympathy. He also notes she went to synagogue for eighteen years and stayed bound until she met Jesus there. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

**v. 14:**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the rabbis let physicians act in emergencies but not for long-term illnesses. The ruler didn't dare challenge Jesus to his face. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- Guzik, quoting Barclay: the ruler spoke to the crowd, not to Jesus, though his words were aimed at Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

**vv. 15–16:**
- The Pulpit Commentary: older manuscripts read the plural "hypocrites", taking in the whole party of men who put ritual in place of holy living. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- Bible Hub's chapter notes: the same Greek verb, "loose", is used for the animals and for the woman, showing equal concern. https://biblehub.com/luke/13.htm
- Guzik: Jesus' wording means she *must* be loosed, not just that she *ought* to be. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

**v. 17:** The Pulpit Commentary: the shaming of the critics and the people's joy led straight into the two parables of the kingdom that follow. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**vv. 18–21:** These verses are read in two opposite ways; see section 2.

**v. 22:** The Pulpit Commentary: Luke's travel note marks this whole section as the last journey toward Jerusalem before the final Passover. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm

**v. 23:**
- Bible.org: the rabbis argued over whether all Jews would be saved on Judgment Day or only certain groups. https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-13
- Matthew Henry: Jesus came to guide consciences, not to satisfy curiosity. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/13-24.html

**v. 24:** The Greek word for "strive" means to struggle or fight (Bible.org: an athletic contest). https://biblehub.com/luke/13.htm ; https://bible.org/seriespage/luke-13
- What the striving means is debated; see section 2.

**vv. 25–27:**
- Precept Austin: the door of mercy will not stay open forever. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-13-commentary
- Wesley reads "I do not know you" as "I do not approve of your ways". https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm
- Guzik: Jesus knew *about* them, but had no relationship with them through faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- Bible Hub's study note: they knew his teaching and ate in his presence, yet did not truly belong to Him. https://biblehub.com/luke/13-24.htm

**v. 28:**
- The Pulpit Commentary: the phrase "weeping and gnashing of teeth" describes the deepest anguish, and appears six times in Matthew. https://biblehub.com/luke/13.htm
- Guzik: being Jewish by birth guaranteed no place in the kingdom, just as being a Gentile was no barrier to it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

**vv. 29–30:**
- 1517 (Lutheran): Jesus doesn't say how many will be saved, but those saved will come from every direction, and no one people owns access to the Master. https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1322-30-pentecost-11-series-c
- Matthew Henry: few will be saved from among those we think most likely. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/13-24.html

**v. 31:** Coffman: Jesus signalled that he knew all about the Pharisees' plans to kill him. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-13.html

**v. 32:** Barclay: Jesus took his orders from God, and would not shorten his work by one day for any earthly king. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/13-3.html

**v. 33:**
- Wesley: Jerusalem claimed a kind of right to murder God's messengers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm
- Coffman: the saying implies Jesus was safer anywhere except Jerusalem. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-13.html

**v. 34:**
- Wesley: Jesus had made three solemn visits to Jerusalem since his baptism for this very purpose. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/wen/luke-13.html
- Coffman thinks the lament was spoken at least twice. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-13.html
- Guzik: the hen shows God's protective, mothering heart. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- What "you were unwilling" says about God's will is debated; see section 2.

**v. 35:** Three readings of the promise:
- **Israel's future repentance.** The Pulpit Commentary: the promise points to the far future, the day of Israel's penitence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
- **Not fulfilled in AD 70.** Guzik takes this verse to mean the Jewish people will remain until Christ returns. He calls the AD 70 reading a wrong interpretation. https://enduringword.com/feed/
- **No promise of seeing Jesus.** Wesley reads it differently: taught by disaster, they would long for a Messiah. He says it does not imply they would then see Jesus at all. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm

---

## 2. Where Protestant traditions really differ

**vv. 18–21, are the mustard seed and the leaven good growth or corruption?**
- **Traditional reading: the kingdom spreads.** The Pulpit Commentary says the mustard seed shows the kingdom's rapid growth from a tiny start. The leaven shows the quiet inner change it works in people, steadily spreading through the world. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/luke/13.htm
  - Bible Hub's summary agrees: the parables show the kingdom's expansive and transformative nature. https://biblehub.com/luke/13.htm
- **Minority reading: corruption in the church.** Guzik (Calvary Chapel, sometimes classed as charismatic) admits the growth reading is the more familiar one, but rejects it:
  - The tree grows unnaturally large, and the birds stand for Satan's agents, as in Matthew 13.
  - Leaven always pictures sin.
  - He quotes G. Campbell Morgan: the leaven is "paganizing influences" brought into the church.
  
  https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- This split follows schools of interpretation more than denominations.

**v. 24, what does "strive" mean?**
- **Methodist (Wesley):** "Strive as in an agony" — just seeking won't do. Then "Agonize, therefore, now by faith, prayer, holiness, patience." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/luke/13.htm
- **Baptist / Reformed (MacArthur):** calls the verse shocking against modern "easy believism", and says the Lord saves no one apart from the will of the sinner. https://www.gty.org/sermons/42-184/are-just-a-few-being-saved-part-1
- **Evangelical (Precept Austin):** endurance doesn't earn salvation. Believers can endure because they are saved, and the Spirit gives the desire and power. https://www.preceptaustin.org/luke-13-commentary
- **Guzik:** the striving isn't a call to save yourself by good works; good works aren't the right gate. Jesus himself is the door. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- **Lutheran (1517):** instead of answering "how many", Jesus points to the one who grants salvation. https://www.1517.org/articles/gospel-luke-1322-30-pentecost-11-series-c

**v. 34, "How often I longed… but you were unwilling"**
- **Calvinist reading (Gill and Ligonier).** Gill, writing on the parallel verse Matthew 23:37, says Christ speaks here as a man, expressing human affection and a wish for Jerusalem's earthly good. Because the wish came "often", it cannot be God's unchanging will, so it does not contradict God's absolute and sovereign will. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/kjv/matthew/23-37.html
  - Ligonier quotes Calvin that God's will is shown in two ways, including a hidden sovereign will governing all that happens. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/jesus-laments-over-jerusalem
- **Human-responsibility reading.**
  - Coffman (Churches of Christ, not Methodist): Christ respected humanity's sovereign will; Israel chose to reject her King. https://studylight.org/commentaries/bcc/luke-13.html
  - Matthew Henry: Christ's willingness makes sinners' unwillingness worse and leaves their blood on their own heads. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/luke/13-34.html
  - Guzik: the problem lay in their unwillingness, not his. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/
- **Wesley's note on this verse** doesn't take up the will question. It only mentions the three visits.

**v. 16, the woman "bound by Satan" and whether believers can be demonized:** Guzik notes this verse is sometimes used to argue that a believer can be possessed. He replies that she was not yet born again, since the cross had not happened. He holds that Christians cannot be possessed because they are new creations. He also quotes Spurgeon: Satan bound her but doesn't seem to have possessed her. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/luke-13/

---

## 3. Other views

**v. 24, Catholic (Haydock, 1811):**
- Quoting Challoner, people want to be saved but fail for want of taking sufficient pains.
- Haydock reads Jesus' answer as a yes: the saved are very few.
- He squares this with v. 29 ("many shall come from east and west"): many, but few compared with the number of the lost.

https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/luke-13.html
